hook: *40%* Refund Pulls Indian Film Money To Australia
dek: AFFI returns with bootcamps pairing Indian producers with Australia's film incentives.

slides.label: What happened
slides.text: The *Australian Film Festival of India* returns after a COVID pause, screening in Indian cities through *Dec. 22*.

slides.label: New Push
slides.text: A new industry strand targets Indian producers and investors as the *India-Australia Co-Production Treaty* kicks in.

slides.label: Bootcamp
slides.text: The *Screen Australia*-backed Australian Cinema Bootcamp runs full day sessions in *Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum*.

slides.label: Who's Involved
slides.text: Festival director *Peter Castaldi* leads it, with advisors like producer *Lori Fesker* and actor *Viveck Vaswani*.

slides.label: The Money
slides.text: Australia's *Producer Offset* refunds *40%* of qualifying local spend, plus state grants lower investor risk.

slides.label: Backing
slides.text: *Disney Studios, Ausfilm*, the City of Perth and UNSW support the festival; Screen Australia backs the bootcamp.

slides.label: On Screen
slides.text: The lineup includes *'First Light'*, Australia's Oscar submission, and *'UnIndian'* starring Brett Lee.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: For Indian and diaspora filmmakers, this treaty opens real funding paths and access to global-level production tools.

question: Will Indian producers flock to Australia for this deal? Yes or no.

caption_instagram:
The Australian Film Festival of India (AFFI) is back after a COVID era pause, bringing real money to the table for Indian producers through the new India-Australia Co-Production Treaty.

Screen Australia is backing a new Australian Cinema Bootcamp running in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum, teaching Indian producers, directors and investors how to tap into Australia's 40% Producer Offset and other state incentives. Festival director Peter Castaldi leads the relaunch, with advisors like Lori Fesker and Viveck Vaswani, and support from Disney Studios, Ausfilm and UNSW. The lineup includes 'First Light,' Australia's Oscar submission, and 'UnIndian' starring Brett Lee.

This is Indian cinema building new global pathways on its own terms, with money, talent and distribution flowing both ways.

Will Indian producers flock to Australia for this deal? Yes or no.

caption_linkedin:
The Australian Film Festival of India has relaunched after a COVID era pause, and the real story is the new industry infrastructure built around it. As the India-Australia Audio Visual Co-Production Treaty takes effect, Screen Australia is running an Australian Cinema Bootcamp in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum aimed squarely at Indian producers, directors, investors and post-production teams.

The pitch is financial as much as creative. Australia's Producer Offset refunds 40% of qualifying local spend on eligible features, and individual states add their own grants, lowering the capital risk for anyone co-producing across borders. Festival director Peter Castaldi is leading the relaunch, backed by an advisory council that includes producer Lori Fesker and actor-producer Viveck Vaswani, with institutional support from Disney Studios, Ausfilm and UNSW.

For producers outside the traditional Hollywood pipeline, treaties like this create real, bankable pathways into international co-production rather than one-off opportunities.

Will this treaty actually move production money between India and Australia? Yes or no.
